bio-001.why: Statins occupy the substrate-binding site of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase. By competing with HMG-CoA, they reduce mevalonate production and slow cholesterol synthesis in the liver.

notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase can phosphorylate and inhibit the reductase when cellular energy is scarce.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, placing it a step removed from the enzyme that binds statins.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes an inhibitory phosphate from the reductase, restoring its activity independently of statin binding.
notes.E: Protein kinase A transmits signals from cyclic AMP, whereas statins bind the enzyme that produces mevalonate.

bio-002.why: When cellular energy is scarce, AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase. This reduces the production of mevalonate and slows the energy-consuming synthesis of cholesterol.

notes.A: The reductase converts HMG-CoA into mevalonate and receives its inhibitory phosphate from a separate kinase.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which then directly phosphorylates the reductase.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphate from HMG-CoA reductase, allowing cholesterol synthesis to resume.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas the enzyme that directly senses energy status and inhibits the reductase is AMP-activated protein kinase.

bio-003.why: An upstream kinase phosphorylates a threonine in the catalytic subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase. This phosphorylation allows the energy sensor to inhibit biosynthetic pathways when energy is scarce.

notes.A: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is a downstream target of the activated energy sensor.
notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase is the enzyme receiving the activating phosphate in this signalling step.
notes.D: The reductase phosphatase restores the activity of the cholesterol-synthesis enzyme by removing its inhibitory phosphate.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas a distinct upstream kinase phosphorylates the activation loop of the energy sensor.

bio-005.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate and the cofactor biotin to convert acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This commits carbon to fatty acid synthesis and controls the supply of two-carbon units for elongation.

notes.A: Condensation takes place on fatty acid synthase once the carboxylase has supplied the malonyl group.
notes.B: Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA, but this also supplies pathways other than fatty acid synthesis.
notes.C: The carboxylase adds bicarbonate-derived carbon to acetyl-CoA, so free malonate is not its starting material.
notes.E: The first reduction on fatty acid synthase consumes NADPH after the chain has already undergone condensation.

bio-006.why: A sustained carbohydrate surplus can provide acetyl-CoA for new fatty acids and glycerol 3-phosphate for their storage as triacylglycerol. Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and esterification in the fed state.

notes.A: Plants also synthesise triacylglycerols, which are an important energy reserve in many seeds.
notes.C: Low carbohydrate availability generally favours oxidation of fatty acids and reduces the use of carbohydrate carbon for new fatty acids.
notes.D: Animals synthesise triacylglycerols in the fed state, including in the liver and adipose tissue.
notes.E: A sustained carbohydrate surplus supplies both carbon and an insulin signal for fat storage in humans.

bio-007.why: Insulin favours storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Glucose supplies glycerol 3-phosphate for the triacylglycerol backbone and can supply acetyl-CoA for synthesis of the attached fatty acids.

notes.A: Fat is stored with little water and yields more energy per gram than hydrated glycogen.
notes.C: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage after feeding, while low insulin favours release of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
notes.D: Mammalian liver can convert surplus glucose into fatty acids and esterify these to form triacylglycerols.
notes.E: Phosphatidate loses its phosphate to form diacylglycerol, which receives a third fatty acyl group.

bio-008.why: In the cytidine diphosphate (CDP) routes, one partner is activated and the other supplies a free hydroxyl group. Linking two CDP-activated partners is unnecessary for forming the phosphodiester bond.

notes.A: CDP-choline transfers its phosphocholine group to diacylglycerol during the formation of phosphatidylcholine.
notes.B: Free inositol reacts with activated CDP-diacylglycerol in the pathway that forms phosphatidylinositol.
notes.D: Mammalian cells can exchange serine for the ethanolamine head group of phosphatidylethanolamine to make phosphatidylserine.
notes.E: The liver can synthesise phosphatidylcholine by adding three methyl groups to the head group of phosphatidylethanolamine.

bio-009.why: Low-density lipoprotein carries much of the cholesterol in plasma as cholesteryl esters. Cells can bind its apolipoprotein B-100 through LDL receptors and take up the particle by endocytosis.

notes.A: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is a remnant that can return to the liver or give rise to low-density lipoprotein.
notes.C: High-density lipoprotein accepts excess cholesterol from peripheral cells and participates in its return to the liver.
notes.D: Chylomicrons chiefly deliver dietary triacylglycerol, and their cholesterol-rich remnants are taken up by the liver.
notes.E: Very-low-density lipoprotein chiefly exports hepatic triacylglycerol and gives rise to cholesterol-enriched particles as it loses fat.

bio-010.why: The liver packages triacylglycerol into very-low-density lipoprotein for export. Lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyses the particle's triacylglycerol in capillaries, making fatty acids available to muscle and adipose tissue.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are rich in triacylglycerol too, but the intestine produces them to transport fat absorbed from a meal.
notes.B: Low-density lipoprotein has already lost much of its precursor's triacylglycerol and is enriched in cholesteryl esters.
notes.D: High-density lipoprotein participates mainly in cholesterol transport and carries a relatively small amount of triacylglycerol.
notes.E: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant formed after lipoprotein lipase has removed some triacylglycerol from the hepatic particle.

bio-011.why: Acetyl-CoA supplies all the carbon atoms retained in cholesterol. Its two-carbon units first form acetoacetyl-CoA and then HMG-CoA, which is reduced to mevalonate in the sterol pathway.

notes.A: Free acetate must first be activated with coenzyme A before it can enter cholesterol synthesis.
notes.C: Oxaloacetate can help export acetyl units as citrate, but is regenerated when cytosolic citrate is cleaved.
notes.D: Malate participates in the citrate shuttle and can help supply reducing power for biosynthesis.
notes.E: Pyruvate can yield acetyl-CoA through oxidative decarboxylation, placing it upstream of the direct building block.

bio-012.why: Cholecystokinin is made by intestinal endocrine cells from a peptide precursor, preprocholecystokinin. The other choices are sterols or products of sterol metabolism.

notes.A: The liver oxidises and shortens the side chain of cholesterol to form primary bile acids, including chenodeoxycholic acid.
notes.B: Glycocholic acid forms when the liver conjugates the cholesterol-derived bile acid cholic acid with glycine.
notes.C: Steroid-producing cells convert cholesterol to pregnenolone, from which they can synthesise testosterone.
notes.D: In skin, ultraviolet B light acts on the sterol precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol to initiate vitamin D₃ synthesis.

bio-015.why: Type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia is an isolated elevation of LDL with relatively normal triglycerides. Reduced receptor-mediated LDL clearance is a classic cause, as in familial hypercholesterolaemia due to an impaired LDL receptor pathway.

notes.A: Increased hepatic production of VLDL would usually raise plasma triglycerides rather than producing an isolated increase in LDL cholesterol.
notes.C: High HDL does not explain an isolated accumulation of LDL particles in type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia.
notes.D: Impaired processing of VLDL would retain more triglyceride-rich particles. It is not the expected mechanism for an isolated LDL elevation.

bio-016.why: Lovastatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Lower intracellular cholesterol can increase expression of functioning LDL receptors, increasing LDL clearance and lowering blood cholesterol. The response is smaller when receptor activity is nearly absent.

notes.A: Lower hepatic cholesterol generally increases expression of residual functional LDL receptors through sterol-sensitive regulation.
notes.B: Lovastatin decreases de novo cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, even though feedback can increase enzyme expression.
notes.C: ACAT esterifies intracellular cholesterol for storage. Increased esterification is not the principal action of lovastatin.
notes.E: Statins usually lower LDL and can also modestly decrease circulating triglyceride concentrations rather than raising them.

bio-017.why: Lipoprotein density increases as the fraction of protein relative to lipid increases. The order from lowest to highest is chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL. The proposed sequences do not follow that order.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are the least dense, but VLDL is less dense than LDL and must come before LDL.
notes.B: HDL has the highest density in this group and follows LDL in the order of increasing density.
notes.C: VLDL is less dense than IDL, because IDL is a smaller remnant left after some triglyceride has been removed.
notes.D: HDL, LDL and VLDL are listed in descending rather than ascending order of density.

bio-020.why: The malonyl/acetyltransferase domain of mammalian fatty acid synthase transfers malonyl from malonyl-CoA to the terminal thiol of ACP's phosphopantetheine arm. The loaded malonyl–ACP supplies a two-carbon unit during condensation.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents for later steps. It does not transfer the malonyl group from CoA.
notes.B: An acyl carrier protein holds the malonyl group as a thioester. The transfer reaction is catalysed by the transferase domain.
notes.C: The mobile ACP arm carries substrates between enzyme sites. Catalysis of malonyl loading requires the distinct transacylase activity.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase uses NADPH after condensation to reduce a carbonyl group. It does not load malonyl onto ACP.

bio-022.why: After condensation, beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce the beta-keto group to a hydroxyl group. This is the first reduction in the fatty acid synthase elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents, but the reduction also requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase to catalyse hydride transfer.
notes.C: Enoyl–ACP reductase acts later on the carbon–carbon double bond. The keto group requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase.
notes.D: ACP carries the intermediate but is neither the reductase nor the reducing cofactor for the keto group.
notes.E: The cycle has two reduction reactions. The later enoyl reductase is not needed for the initial conversion of the keto group to an alcohol.

bio-023.why: After dehydration makes a trans-enoyl–ACP intermediate, enoyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce its carbon–carbon double bond. This yields a saturated acyl–ACP ready for another elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH donates reducing equivalents, but the enoyl reductase is required to transfer them to the double bond.
notes.B: Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts earlier on the carbonyl group, before dehydration produces the enoyl intermediate.
notes.D: ACP can hold the enoyl intermediate, but it does not supply reducing equivalents or replace enoyl–ACP reductase.
notes.E: Both reductases use NADPH in the overall cycle. Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts at a separate earlier step.

bio-024.why: NADPH provides the reducing equivalents for both reductive steps of mammalian fatty acid synthesis. One NADPH reduces the beta-keto group and another reduces the double bond in each elongation cycle.

notes.B: An acyl carrier protein binds and carries growing intermediates. It does not donate the electrons required for reduction.
notes.C: An ACP domain is a carrier with a phosphopantetheine arm, rather than the source of reducing equivalents.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase catalyses reduction but obtains the reducing equivalents it transfers from NADPH.
notes.E: The transacylase loads acetyl and malonyl groups. It is not the source of reducing equivalents.

bio-027.why: Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia is caused by defective clearance of cholesterol-rich remnants, often associated with an apoE variant such as apoE2. The accumulated remnant particles carry both triglyceride and cholesterol, so both can be elevated.

notes.A: The intestine can still make chylomicrons after eating. The defect involves clearance of remnant particles rather than absence of chylomicron production.
notes.B: Remnants derived from VLDL can accumulate, so normal VLDL-related lipid handling is not typical of the disorder.
notes.C: Retained triglyceride-rich remnants contribute to elevated triglyceride levels rather than an isolated normal triglyceride result.
notes.D: Cholesterol carried in accumulating remnant particles is often elevated, along with triglycerides.

bio-028.why: In the principal endoplasmic-reticulum elongation system, malonyl-CoA is the immediate donor of the two carbons added to the acyl chain. Acetyl-CoA is upstream as a source of malonyl-CoA, rather than the immediate donor in the elongase reaction.

notes.A: Each elongation round uses condensation, reduction, dehydration and a second reduction, analogous to the sequence of fatty acid synthase.
notes.B: The major elongase system for long-chain acyl-CoAs is associated with the endoplasmic reticulum.
notes.C: One elongation round can convert a 16-carbon palmitoyl-CoA to an 18-carbon product, stearoyl-CoA.
notes.D: Malonyl-CoA is a substrate for the endoplasmic-reticulum elongase and supplies the added carbons after decarboxylation.

bio-030.why: A large meal supplies triglyceride that enterocytes package into chylomicrons. At about three hours after eating, these triglyceride-rich particles can increase circulating triglycerides. LDL and HDL cholesterol usually change less acutely.

notes.B: Postprandial dietary lipid is carried mainly in chylomicrons. A sharp immediate rise in LDL cholesterol is not the characteristic effect.
notes.C: HDL cholesterol usually does not fall sharply after a single meal in a healthy person. Triglyceride-rich particles change more.
notes.D: VLDL is produced in the liver, while the new postprandial particles come from the intestine. A sharp fall in VLDL is not the expected change.

bio-304.why: The Friedewald equation has long been used to estimate LDL cholesterol and can work reasonably in appropriate samples. Its simplifying assumptions can cause error at high triglyceride concentrations or very low LDL. Those limitations do not explain its widespread use.

notes.A: Both statements can be true, but the unmodelled factors explain potential error rather than why the calculation is useful.
notes.C: The equation has practical limitations because the triglyceride-to-cholesterol ratio in VLDL is not constant across samples.
notes.D: The long-standing use of the estimate in appropriate settings is real, even though newer equations can improve accuracy.
notes.E: The estimate is widely used historically, and the concern about unaccounted sources of error is also valid.

bio-305.why: Very high triglycerides can cause acute pancreatitis. A proposed mechanism is that chylomicron-rich blood impairs pancreatic microcirculation and lipases release locally injurious free fatty acids. Ischaemia and local acidosis can reinforce the injury.

notes.B: The reason provides a recognised mechanism that can connect severe triglyceride elevation to pancreatic tissue injury.
notes.C: Capillary flow changes and free-fatty-acid toxicity are plausible contributors to the link, even though they may not account for every case.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia is an established cause of acute pancreatitis, so the assertion is not false.
notes.E: Both the association and the proposed microvascular and lipotoxic explanation have physiological support.

bio-310.why: Vertebrate cytosolic fatty acid synthase is a type I synthase. Each polypeptide contains multiple catalytic domains and an ACP domain, and two polypeptides associate to form the functional complex that commonly produces palmitate.

notes.A: Separate proteins carry out the individual reactions of type II synthase systems. The vertebrate cytosolic enzyme combines the activities in one polypeptide.
notes.B: Cytosolic fatty acid synthase is encoded by a nuclear gene, rather than by the mitochondrial genome.
notes.C: The major pathway for de novo palmitate production is cytosolic. Mitochondria have a distinct specialised synthesis system.
notes.E: Multiple enzyme activities assembled in one protein chain are a defining feature of the vertebrate type I synthase.

bio-313.why: Lovastatin is a statin. Its active form competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing mevalonate formation and hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

notes.A: Clofibrate is a fibrate that acts mainly through PPAR-alpha to change expression of lipid metabolism genes.
notes.B: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate used to lower triglycerides. Its principal mechanism does not involve direct inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.D: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut and increases their faecal loss. It does not directly inhibit the reductase.
notes.E: Lovastatin has a well-defined direct inhibitory action at the reductase substrate-binding site.

bio-314.why: Simvastatin inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase, which lowers intracellular cholesterol and increases LDL receptor expression. The resulting decline in circulating LDL reduces the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events.

notes.A: Low-dose niacin is not standard drug therapy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk reduction. Lipid effects from pharmacological niacin do not substitute for established statin benefit.
notes.B: High-dose vitamin C is not an established substitute for LDL-lowering therapy to reduce atherosclerotic events.
notes.C: Bariatric surgery can improve some cardiovascular risk factors in selected patients, but it is a procedure rather than the drug treatment asked for.
notes.D: Dietary modification contributes to risk reduction. It is a lifestyle intervention rather than a medication.

bio-317.why: Liver-derived VLDL contains one apoB-100 molecule per particle. ApoB-100 is the structural scaffold and remains with the particle as it is converted to IDL and, for some particles, LDL.

notes.B: ApoB-48 is a shorter product expressed in the intestine and is the structural protein of chylomicrons.
notes.C: ApoA-I is the principal structural apolipoprotein of HDL, rather than the scaffold of VLDL.
notes.D: ApoC-II can be carried on VLDL and activates lipoprotein lipase. It is exchangeable and not the main structural protein.
notes.E: ApoE helps hepatic receptors recognise some triglyceride-rich remnants. It is not the fixed structural scaffold of VLDL.

bio-318.why: Persistently elevated VLDL can increase exposure to atherogenic apoB-containing remnant particles. Smaller VLDL remnants can enter and be retained in the arterial wall, contributing to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

notes.B: VLDL and its remnants carry cholesterol as well as triglyceride. Persistent elevation does not characteristically cause low blood cholesterol.
notes.C: Hepatosplenomegaly can occur in severe chylomicronaemia or other disorders. It is not the principal long-term consequence of chronically raised VLDL.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia can cause abdominal pain from pancreatitis. Atherosclerosis is the key long-term vascular consequence of increased atherogenic remnants.
notes.E: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency can cause triglyceride-rich particles to accumulate. It is a possible underlying disorder, rather than a consequence of increased VLDL.

bio-319.why: Many lipidoses are inherited storage disorders in which a defect in lipid degradation causes particular substrates to accumulate. Demonstration of reduced activity of the relevant enzyme can support the diagnosis, sometimes together with genetic and biomarker tests.

notes.A: Classic lipid storage disorders are usually inherited rather than acquired during life.
notes.B: The substrate typically accumulates because it cannot be degraded normally. Its concentration may rise in affected tissue rather than fall.
notes.C: These disorders can affect nervous tissue, liver and other organs. They do not generally cause ordinary obesity by lipid accumulation in the stomach.
notes.E: Some accumulated lipids or derivatives can be detected in body fluids and serve as useful biomarkers, depending on the disorder.

bio-321.why: Statins lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis and increase expression of functioning hepatic LDL receptors. This increases clearance of circulating LDL and usually lowers LDL cholesterol during treatment.

notes.A: A rise in total blood cholesterol is not the expected response when the major LDL cholesterol fraction is being lowered.
notes.B: Statins act chiefly on cholesterol synthesis and LDL clearance, not by lowering blood glucose.
notes.D: Fatty acid beta-oxidation is a separate pathway. Reduced oxidation is not the usual marker of an effective statin response.
notes.E: Hepatic LDL uptake normally increases during statin treatment, so circulating LDL tends to fall rather than rise.

bio-322.why: ApoC-II normally activates lipoprotein lipase. When apoC-II is deficient, triglycerides in chylomicrons are cleared poorly, producing severe hypertriglyceridaemia. This can resemble inherited lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

notes.A: Type I hyperlipoproteinaemia is defined primarily by accumulation of chylomicrons rather than an isolated postprandial increase in VLDL.
notes.B: Failure to activate lipoprotein lipase impairs removal of circulating triglyceride, so a normal triglyceride level is not the expected hallmark.
notes.D: Chylomicrons carry some cholesterol, but the most characteristic change is a major elevation of triglycerides.
notes.E: Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity decreases triglyceride clearance, so triglyceride-rich particles remain in plasma.

bio-324.why: HDL is richest in protein relative to lipid and has the greatest density among these particles. The density then decreases through LDL and VLDL, with triglyceride-rich chylomicrons least dense.

notes.A: LDL is denser than VLDL and must precede it when the particles are listed from most to least dense.
notes.C: HDL has greater density than LDL and chylomicrons, so it belongs at the beginning rather than after them.
notes.D: VLDL is less dense than LDL and HDL. Chylomicrons are the least dense, so they belong at the end.

bio-391.why: Atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima of medium and large arteries. Retained apoB-containing lipoproteins and subsequent inflammatory and fibrous responses contribute to plaque formation. The defining process does not take place in capillary walls.

notes.A: Both claims misidentify capillaries as the site of disease. Plaques form in the arterial intima rather than beneath an outer capillary lining.
notes.B: The vessel and layer descriptions are both inaccurate, so neither claim supplies a valid explanation.
notes.C: Plaque-related thickening involves arteries, not capillaries. The assertion therefore misstates the affected vessels.
notes.D: Lipid retention occurs in the arterial intima. The reason is also inaccurate because it places the lesion in capillaries.

bio-443.why: A total plasma cholesterol above 7.0 mmol/L is markedly elevated among these choices. Clinical decisions also depend on the LDL cholesterol value, family history and other findings, rather than total cholesterol alone.

notes.B: Low bile acid concentrations can affect intestinal fat handling. They are not a plasma cholesterol measurement.
notes.C: Fat malabsorption can result from several digestive disorders. It does not itself indicate markedly elevated plasma cholesterol.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase participates in cholesterol synthesis. Deficiency of the enzyme is not a measured high cholesterol level.
notes.E: An absence of a heart attack does not exclude high plasma cholesterol. Cholesterol is measured directly.

bio-444.why: Bile salts help stabilise small lipid droplets and form mixed micelles that carry lipid digestion products. Low delivery of bile salts to the intestine can impair emulsification and make fat absorption less efficient.

notes.A: High plasma cholesterol measures a circulating lipid concentration. It does not show that too few bile salts reach the intestinal lumen.
notes.C: Impaired fat absorption can follow defective emulsification. It is a possible result rather than the upstream loss of an emulsifying agent.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is part of cholesterol synthesis, but the most direct defect here is reduced intestinal availability of bile salts.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not explain how dietary fat is dispersed in the intestine.

bio-445.why: Poor emulsification can limit access of lipases to dietary fat and can accompany insufficient mixed-micelle formation. This reduces absorption of long-chain lipid products and can lead to fatty stools and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

notes.A: Defective emulsification directly affects intestinal lipid processing. A high plasma cholesterol level is not its expected presentation.
notes.B: A low bile salt supply can cause defective emulsification. It is an upstream factor rather than the resulting problem with nutrient uptake.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is involved in cholesterol synthesis. Deficient activity is not a clinical manifestation diagnostic of low emulsification.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not indicate whether dietary fat is being digested and absorbed.

bio-458.why: Carrots are plant foods and are not a meaningful dietary source of cholesterol. Plant tissues primarily contain phytosterols. Butter, cheese and egg yolk are animal foods that contribute cholesterol.

notes.A: Butter contains dairy fat and can provide dietary cholesterol, although the amount depends on the serving.
notes.B: Cheese is made from milk and contains some cholesterol, with variation according to fat content and serving size.
notes.C: Egg yolk contains cholesterol in its lipid fraction, in contrast to typical plant foods.

bio-903.why: Bile salts are derived from cholesterol. Hepatocytes convert the sterol into primary bile acids, which can be conjugated with glycine or taurine before secretion into bile.

notes.B: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids built from ceramide and an oligosaccharide that contains sialic acid.
notes.C: Geraniol is a monoterpene alcohol formed from isoprenoid precursors. It is not made by modifying a sterol.
notes.D: Phosphatidylglycerol is a glycerophospholipid with a glycerol head group. Its backbone is not cholesterol.
notes.E: Prostaglandins are eicosanoids formed from polyunsaturated fatty acids, often arachidonic acid.

bio-904.why: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, slowing conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Lower hepatic cholesterol increases LDL receptor expression, which promotes removal of LDL from blood.

notes.B: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triglycerides in circulating particles. It is not the direct enzyme target of statins.
notes.C: The direct drug effect is inhibition of the reductase, even though feedback can increase expression of the enzyme.
notes.D: Lower plasma LDL reflects increased hepatic clearance through LDL receptors. Direct blockade of LDL particle synthesis is not the main mechanism.
notes.E: Some statins modestly change HDL cholesterol, but inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase is the defining drug action.

bio-031.why: Antioxidants inhibit oxidation by removing reactive species, interrupting radical chain reactions or preventing reactive species from forming. The exact mechanism depends on the particular antioxidant.

notes.A: A substance that promotes radical formation is acting as a pro-oxidant under those conditions.

bio-032.why: Antioxidant activity depends on a compound's structure and on conditions around it. The local redox state, oxygen availability and transition metals can change which reactions occur and whether the compound has a net antioxidant effect.

notes.A: Molecular structure affects how readily a compound can donate electrons, stabilise a radical or enter a particular cellular compartment.
notes.B: The local redox state can affect whether the compound is available in a form that scavenges reactive species or is regenerated after reacting.
notes.C: Oxygen and transition metals influence radical formation and can change the net effect of a compound in a particular environment.

bio-033.why: Free radicals can damage many classes of cell molecules. They initiate lipid peroxidation, oxidise proteins and carbohydrates, and modify DNA bases or the sugar–phosphate backbone.

notes.A: Radicals can attack polyunsaturated fatty acids and initiate a chain reaction of membrane lipid peroxidation.
notes.B: Oxidative attack can modify carbohydrates, including the deoxyribose backbone in DNA and sugars in other cell structures.
notes.C: Oxidation can modify amino acid side chains and alter the structure, stability or activity of proteins.
notes.D: Reactive species can modify DNA bases and contribute to strand breaks or other lesions.

bio-034.why: Carotenoids have extended systems of conjugated double bonds. These allow them to accept excitation energy from singlet oxygen and dissipate it, usually as heat, returning oxygen toward its ground state.

notes.A: How widely a pigment occurs in nature does not explain its molecular capacity to quench singlet oxygen.
notes.C: Methyl groups can influence overall structure, but the extended conjugated system is the key feature for efficient energy transfer.
notes.D: The conjugated electron system provides a recognised mechanism for singlet oxygen quenching.

bio-035.why: Antioxidant systems limit damage by removing reactive oxygen species or interrupting the reactions they start. This can protect cell components without blocking the ordinary use of oxygen in aerobic metabolism.

notes.A: Antioxidants do not generally block aerobic pathways by binding molecular oxygen. They target specific reactive intermediates or their reactions.
notes.B: Deliberately increasing radical formation is a pro-oxidant effect. It is not the usual protective action of antioxidants.
notes.D: Some vitamins themselves participate in antioxidant systems. Generating reactive oxygen species by complexing with vitamins is not the general mechanism.

bio-037.why: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen. Catalase and peroxidases then remove hydrogen peroxide, so water is not the direct product of superoxide dismutase.

notes.A: Mitochondrial electron transfer can reduce oxygen one electron at a time and produce superoxide.
notes.B: Superoxide has an unpaired electron and is classified as a radical reactive oxygen species.
notes.D: Superoxide can participate in metal-catalysed production of hydroxyl radical from hydrogen peroxide. The direct uncatalysed reaction is very slow.

bio-039.why: Red cells use G6PD to generate NADPH and maintain reduced glutathione. Certain oxidant antimalarials can trigger haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency, causing dark urine from free haemoglobin. Malaria itself can also cause haemolysis.

notes.A: Acute nephritis can cause dark urine from red cells in the urine. The timing after an oxidant exposure raises concern for haemolysis in this vignette.
notes.C: Hepatitis can darken urine through conjugated bilirubin, but that differs mechanistically from the possible haemoglobinuria after oxidative red-cell injury.
notes.D: Haematuria means intact red cells are present in urine. Intravascular haemolysis can instead release free haemoglobin into urine.

bio-042.why: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce the disulphide bond of oxidised glutathione. This regenerates two reduced glutathione molecules for use in antioxidant reactions.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove peroxides, forming oxidised glutathione in the process.
notes.B: The standard enzyme that regenerates reduced glutathione from its disulphide is glutathione reductase. This reaction uses NADPH.
notes.D: Glutathione synthetase forms glutathione by adding glycine during biosynthesis. It does not reduce oxidised glutathione.

bio-043.why: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to produce hypochlorous acid in phagocytes. Its characteristic role is to generate a reactive antimicrobial oxidant, unlike antioxidant systems that remove superoxide or peroxides.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove hydrogen peroxide or lipid hydroperoxides.
notes.B: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, limiting peroxide accumulation.
notes.C: Superoxide dismutase converts the superoxide radical to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen so other enzymes can handle the peroxide.

bio-044.why: Glutathione is a reducing substrate rather than the catalyst. Glutathione peroxidase catalyses peroxide reduction using reduced glutathione, which is oxidised in the process.

notes.A: Different superoxide dismutase forms occur in the cytosol and mitochondria, protecting those cellular compartments.
notes.B: Dismutation of superoxide produces hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen.
notes.C: Catalase removes hydrogen peroxide through a reaction that produces water and molecular oxygen.

bio-045.why: DNA can be damaged by reactive oxygen species. Oxidation can generate modified bases such as 8-oxoguanine and contribute to strand breaks, so antioxidant defences and DNA repair are important.

notes.A: Healthy cells have systems that balance the production and removal of reactive species and maintain a suitable redox environment.
notes.B: Mitochondrial metabolism can generate hydrogen peroxide, some of which can reach the cytosol and participate in redox signalling.
notes.C: The KEAP1–NRF2 system senses changes in oxidative and electrophilic stress and regulates expression of protective genes.

bio-046.why: The hydroxyl radical reacts extremely rapidly with many nearby molecules, including lipids, proteins and DNA. It often causes damage near the site where it forms because its lifetime is so short.

notes.B: Superoxide is a radical that participates in redox reactions, but it is generally less reactive toward many targets than hydroxyl radical.
notes.C: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but not a free radical because it has no unpaired electron.
notes.D: Organic oxygen-centred radicals can participate in oxidative reactions. Hydroxyl radical is usually the most rapidly reacting species among these choices.

bio-047.why: Different antioxidants protect different compartments or act at different stages of oxidation. Some remove peroxides, while others interrupt lipid radical chains or regenerate the active form of another antioxidant.

notes.B: A single antioxidant does not protect equally against all oxidants or in every cellular compartment.

bio-048.why: Oxidative stress can damage proteins, nucleic acids or other targets without producing detectable lipid peroxidation. The absence of one marker therefore does not rule out redox imbalance.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation is only one potential result of oxidative stress. Other targets can be damaged even when this marker is absent.

bio-050.why: Lipid peroxidation can produce reactive aldehydes that form DNA adducts or alter signalling. These effects can contribute to mutations or processes associated with tumour development, although peroxidation alone does not determine whether cancer occurs.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation can have effects beyond the membrane. Its reactive products can modify DNA and participate in processes that contribute to oncogenesis.

bio-052.why: DNA injury can activate cellular stress pathways that change mitochondrial or enzyme activity and lead to additional reactive oxygen species. Oxidative species can also cause DNA damage, so the association can operate in both directions.

notes.B: DNA damage is not only an outcome of oxidative stress. A damage response can also increase oxidant generation in some settings.

bio-053.why: Reactive oxygen species can arise during normal metabolism, including mitochondrial electron transfer. Disease and tissue injury can increase their formation through inflammatory or metal-catalysed reactions, including reactions involving hydrogen peroxide.

notes.A: Normal metabolism is a source, but disease and tissue injury can also change oxidant production.
notes.B: Endogenous metabolism and peroxide-related reactions are relevant, and damaged tissue can also contribute to reactive species formation.
notes.C: A focus on disease and damage omits the low-level oxidant production that occurs in normal cellular metabolism.
notes.D: Normal metabolism and injured tissue are sources. Hydrogen peroxide can also give rise to more reactive species through metal-catalysed reactions.

bio-054.why: Reactive oxygen species can originate in several cellular compartments. Mitochondrial electron transfer is a common source, while oxidant-generating enzymes and redox reactions can contribute in the cytoplasm and nuclear region.

notes.A: The nucleus can experience local generation of oxidants, but mitochondria and cytosolic reactions can also contribute.
notes.B: Mitochondria are a major source, but reactive oxygen species are not generated exclusively in mitochondria.
notes.C: Nuclear and mitochondrial sources are possible. Cytoplasmic enzyme reactions can also contribute to oxidant formation.
notes.D: Cytoplasmic and mitochondrial sources are well recognised. Redox-active processes in the nuclear region can also generate reactive species.

bio-055.why: Coffee contains phenolic compounds, almonds provide vitamin E, and many mushrooms contain compounds such as ergothioneine. Each can supply substances with antioxidant properties, although amounts and biological effects differ.

notes.A: Coffee contributes compounds such as chlorogenic acids. Almonds and mushrooms also contain compounds with antioxidant properties.
notes.B: Coffee and almonds both contribute antioxidant compounds, and some mushrooms are a dietary source of ergothioneine.
notes.C: Almonds and mushrooms supply antioxidant compounds. Coffee also contains phenolic substances rather than supplying caffeine alone.
notes.D: Coffee and mushrooms contribute antioxidant compounds. Almonds are also a source of vitamin E and other dietary antioxidants.

bio-056.why: Extracellular proteins can limit oxidation by keeping redox-active metals or haem away from vulnerable molecules. Lactoferrin binds iron, ceruloplasmin oxidises ferrous iron for safe transport, and haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin.

notes.A: Lactoferrin limits the availability of free iron. Ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin also help limit metal- or haem-associated oxidation.
notes.B: Ceruloplasmin has ferroxidase activity that supports iron handling, but it is one of several extracellular protective proteins.
notes.C: Sequestering iron and supporting safer iron transport are protective. Haptoglobin adds a separate defence by binding free haemoglobin.
notes.D: Ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin limit oxidative injury in different ways. Lactoferrin adds protection by binding iron.

bio-059.why: Oxidative attack can modify amino acid side chains, cleave a protein backbone or cause cross-linking. These molecular changes can impair function and make damaged proteins more susceptible to cellular degradation.

notes.B: Radical injury can change the protein molecule itself and can promote degradation of the damaged protein.

bio-060.why: Human cells synthesise glutathione from amino acids, and urate is generated during purine breakdown. Humans lack a functional final enzyme for vitamin C synthesis and must obtain it from the diet.

notes.A: Glutathione is produced internally, but human purine catabolism also produces urate.
notes.C: Urate is formed in the body, whereas vitamin C must normally come from food. This pair also omits glutathione.
notes.D: Both glutathione and urate are made internally. Vitamin C is excluded because humans cannot complete its biosynthesis.

bio-325.why: In the usual model of paraquat toxicity, cellular reductases transfer electrons to paraquat using reduced cofactors. Reduced paraquat then transfers an electron to molecular oxygen, generating superoxide, rather than using superoxide as its normal electron donor.

notes.A: Paraquat participates in repeated reduction and oxidation, which is the basis of its redox activity.
notes.B: Ingestion can result in systemic absorption, although only a portion of the dose is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.
notes.D: Lung cells, including pneumocytes, can be injured by reactive species generated during paraquat redox cycling.
notes.E: The cycle transfers reducing equivalents from cellular cofactors to oxygen, resulting in the formation of superoxide.

bio-332.why: Free radicals can originate in several cellular compartments. Mitochondrial electron transfer can generate superoxide, membrane-associated oxidases can generate reactive species, and reactions involving redox-active metals in lysosomes can form radicals.

notes.B: Lysosomes and membrane-associated reactions can generate radicals, but mitochondrial electron transfer is also a major source.
notes.C: Cell membranes and mitochondria are important sites. Iron-dependent reactions in lysosomes can also contribute.
notes.D: Lysosomal chemistry can generate radicals under some conditions, but radicals can also originate at membranes and inside mitochondria.
notes.E: The cell contains multiple sites capable of generating radicals, including mitochondria and some membrane-bound enzyme systems.

bio-333.why: X-ray exposure can damage proteins during crystallography, in part through radiolysis and reactive species. Oxidation can also alter cellular receptors or antibodies, so antibodies are not inherently protected from oxidative impairment.

notes.A: The claim that antibody activity cannot be altered is too strong. Oxidation can change antigen binding or other antibody properties.
notes.C: Oxidative injury can impair receptors, but antibodies can also be affected. This grouping incorrectly excludes radiation-related protein damage.
notes.D: X-ray damage to a protein is possible, and radical attack can also impair normal receptor function.
notes.E: Radiation-induced protein damage and functional impairment of oxidised receptors are both recognised processes.

bio-334.why: Coffee can supply phenolic compounds, almonds are a source of vitamin E, and mushrooms can contain ergothioneine. All three can contribute dietary compounds with antioxidant properties, with amounts varying by food and preparation.

notes.B: Coffee and almonds provide antioxidant compounds. Mushrooms can also contribute compounds such as ergothioneine.
notes.C: Almonds and mushrooms are examples, but coffee also contains compounds such as chlorogenic acids.
notes.D: Coffee is a source of phenolics. Almonds provide vitamin E, and mushrooms can also contain antioxidant compounds.
notes.E: Each of the three foods contains compounds with antioxidant properties, although that does not establish clinical benefit from a given serving.

bio-335.why: Alpha-tocopherol is a lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant that protects cell membrane lipids from peroxidation. In this comparison, circulating urate and transferrin are classically discussed as extracellular defences. Alpha-tocopherol is also transported in plasma lipoproteins.

notes.A: Plasma urate scavenges some oxidants and transferrin binds iron, so the complete group is not usually classified as intracellular.
notes.B: Urate is a prominent antioxidant in extracellular fluid, while alpha-tocopherol protects the lipid compartment of cell membranes.
notes.D: Urate contributes strongly to circulating antioxidant capacity. The membrane-localised antioxidant among these choices is alpha-tocopherol.
notes.E: Alpha-tocopherol can act in a cellular compartment by interrupting oxidation chains within membranes.

bio-336.why: A hydroxyl radical can start lipid peroxidation by abstracting hydrogen from a lipid. The lipid radical reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical. Breakdown of subsequent lipid hydroperoxides can generate alkoxyl radicals.

notes.A: A lipid radical reacts with oxygen initially to form a lipid peroxyl radical. Alkoxyl radicals may form later when hydroperoxides decompose.

bio-395.why: Carrots, oranges and watermelon contain nutrients such as carotenoids or vitamin C. Botanically, a carrot is a storage root, whereas oranges and watermelons are fruits. Their chemistry, rather than a single food classification, accounts for their nutrient content.

notes.A: The nutrient assertion is reasonable, but the classification of all three as fruits is incorrect.
notes.B: The reason is not true for carrots, which are edible storage roots.
notes.D: The assertion is supported by their nutrient content, while the reason misclassifies carrots as fruit.
notes.E: The fruit classification is inaccurate, but these foods do contain vitamins and compounds with antioxidant properties.

bio-423.why: Oxidative stress is associated with Parkinson disease, including lipid oxidation and depletion of reduced glutathione in the substantia nigra. Changes in oxidised glutathione are less consistent and depend on the tissue and measurement.

notes.A: Increased lipid oxidation products have been reported in Parkinson disease, consistent with oxidative injury to membranes.
notes.B: Mitochondrial dysfunction, dopamine metabolism and other factors can contribute to oxidative stress in affected tissue.
notes.C: A consistent decrease in oxidised glutathione is not established. Nigral studies have often highlighted depletion of the reduced form.
notes.D: Reduced glutathione is often decreased in the substantia nigra. An increase is not the characteristic observation.

bio-456.why: Gamma-glutamylcysteine is combined with glycine to form glutathione. Reduced glutathione supplies reducing equivalents to peroxidases, helping remove hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides before they cause oxidative damage.

notes.B: Glutathione helps maintain the cell's redox environment by reducing oxidants. The protection described is against oxidative damage.

bio-457.why: Oxidative stress is a disturbance in redox control in which oxidant generation exceeds the ability of antioxidant systems to handle it. The resulting reactions can damage lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

notes.B: Toxicity is a broad term for harmful effects. Oxidative stress specifically describes the imbalance between oxidants and antioxidant capacity.

bio-459.why: Cytochrome P450 reactions can leak electrons, activated phagocytes can make superoxide, and alloxan can undergo redox cycling. Lipid peroxidation also propagates radical intermediates, so each of the listed processes can contribute to free radicals.

notes.A: Uncoupled cytochrome P450 activity can release reactive species during electron transfer to oxygen.
notes.B: Activated phagocytes produce superoxide through an NADPH oxidase-dependent respiratory burst.
notes.C: Alloxan can generate reactive species through redox cycling and contribute to oxidative injury.
notes.D: Lipid peroxidation is a chain reaction in which lipid and lipid peroxyl radicals are formed.

bio-061.why: Ribosomes incorporate mainly L-alpha amino acids, with glycine as an achiral exception. Alpha means the amino group is on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group.

notes.A: The usual amino acids in ribosomally synthesised proteins have their amino group at the alpha carbon, rather than the beta carbon.
notes.B: D-beta amino acids differ in both configuration and amino group position from the usual building blocks of proteins.
notes.D: D-alpha amino acids can occur in some biological molecules, but ordinary ribosomal protein synthesis predominantly incorporates the L forms.
notes.E: The structural and stereochemical requirements distinguish the usual protein building blocks from the other amino acid classes.

bio-062.why: Serine has an uncharged, polar hydroxyl-containing side chain at physiological pH. Lysine and arginine have basic side chains, while glutamate has an acidic carboxylate side chain.

notes.A: The guanidinium side chain of arginine is positively charged at physiological pH and is classified as basic.
notes.B: Lysine has an additional amino group in its side chain. It tends to be protonated and positively charged at physiological pH.
notes.D: Glutamate has a second carboxyl group in its side chain, which is usually negatively charged at physiological pH.

bio-063.why: The primary sequence is held together by peptide bonds. These covalent amide bonds join the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of the next.

notes.A: Disulphide bonds can link two cysteine side chains and stabilise folded structure. They do not join every successive amino acid.
notes.C: Peptide bonds are covalent. The more specific name for the bond linking adjacent residues in a protein backbone is a peptide bond.
notes.D: Hydrogen bonding stabilises folding patterns such as alpha helices and beta sheets. It does not make the primary backbone linkage.

bio-064.why: Alpha helices and beta sheets are stabilised largely by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens. The arrangements differ in where the participating peptide groups lie along the chain.

notes.A: Disulphide bridges join cysteine side chains and often support higher levels of folding. They do not form the common backbone pattern of secondary structure.
notes.B: Peptide bonds join amino acids to make the primary backbone. Hydrogen bonds between peptide groups stabilise recurring secondary structures.
notes.D: Covalent bonds make up the chain itself. Alpha helices and beta sheets are distinguished by the pattern of backbone hydrogen bonds.

bio-065.why: Cystinuria impairs tubular reabsorption of cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, ornithine and arginine. Tryptophan is a neutral aromatic amino acid and does not use this affected transport system.

notes.A: Poorly soluble cystine can accumulate in urine and form stones when its tubular reabsorption is impaired.
notes.B: Lysine is a dibasic amino acid normally transported by the affected system and can be increased in urine.
notes.C: Ornithine is one of the dibasic substrates whose proximal tubular uptake is defective in cystinuria.

bio-066.why: The two nitrogen atoms in urea come from different sources. One enters as free ammonia, incorporated into carbamoyl phosphate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. The other is donated by aspartate during argininosuccinate formation.

notes.A: Ornithine accepts the carbamoyl group but is regenerated by arginase. It does not supply the second nitrogen of urea.
notes.B: Aspartate donates one nitrogen, but ornithine cycles through the pathway. The other nitrogen arrives via carbamoyl phosphate.
notes.C: Glutamate can supply ammonia or amino groups upstream. The immediate nitrogen donors are carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate.
notes.E: Carbamoyl phosphate supplies one nitrogen. Aspartate, rather than glutamate directly, supplies the second.

bio-067.why: N-acetylglutamate is the obligatory allosteric activator of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. It increases the liver's ability to incorporate ammonia nitrogen into the urea cycle.

notes.B: AMP is a nucleotide, rather than the enzyme activated by N-acetylglutamate in ureogenesis.
notes.C: Ornithine transcarbamylase uses carbamoyl phosphate in the next reaction. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the direct target of N-acetylglutamate.

bio-068.why: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I catalyses the first committed reaction of ureogenesis in liver mitochondria. It uses ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP, and its activity depends on the allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate.

notes.B: Ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine after carbamoyl phosphate has been made.
notes.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase uses aspartate to supply the second nitrogen in the cytosolic portion of the cycle.
notes.D: Argininosuccinate lyase forms arginine and fumarate downstream of the major regulatory reaction.
notes.E: Arginase releases urea in the final reaction and regenerates ornithine. It is not the principal entry-point regulator.

bio-069.why: The two nitrogen atoms of urea enter through the mitochondrial ammonia–ammonium pool and through the amino group of aspartate. The first is incorporated into carbamoyl phosphate, and aspartate donates the other nitrogen during argininosuccinate synthesis.

notes.A: Glutamine can carry nitrogen to the liver and release it as ammonia. It is not the immediate amino-group donor in argininosuccinate synthesis.
notes.C: Glutamate can supply nitrogen through deamination or transamination, but aspartate is the second direct donor to the cycle.
notes.D: Glutamate is an important upstream nitrogen source. The two immediate inputs are the ammonia–ammonium pool and aspartate.

bio-070.why: Hepatic alanine aminotransferase transfers alanine's amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and pyruvate. The liver can use the pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and dispose of the transferred nitrogen through the urea cycle.

notes.A: Glutamate is the product formed when alpha-ketoglutarate accepts the amino group from alanine.
notes.B: Glutamine can carry nitrogen between tissues, but it is not the keto acid that accepts nitrogen in the hepatic alanine aminotransferase reaction.
notes.D: Aspartate is an important nitrogen donor in the urea cycle. It is not the immediate acceptor used by alanine aminotransferase in this reaction.

bio-071.why: Aspartate aminotransferase interconverts aspartate and oxaloacetate. Fumarate produced in the urea cycle can feed into malate and oxaloacetate, which can regenerate the aspartate required by the cycle.

notes.A: Glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate also participate in nitrogen transfer, but the fumarate-to-aspartate link specifically uses oxaloacetate.
notes.C: Alanine and pyruvate are central to the glucose–alanine cycle between muscle and liver. They are not the pair used in the fumarate–aspartate link.
notes.D: The aspartate–oxaloacetate pair provides a direct way to connect urea cycle nitrogen donation with TCA-linked carbon intermediates.

bio-072.why: Argininosuccinate lyase produces fumarate during the urea cycle. Fumarate is a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate and can be converted to malate and oxaloacetate, linking the pathways.

notes.A: The urea cycle does not directly supply a standard glycolytic intermediate. Its direct carbon link in this comparison is fumarate.
notes.B: The hexose monophosphate shunt uses sugar phosphates, starting with glucose 6-phosphate. Fumarate is not an intermediate of that pathway.
notes.D: Fumarate-derived carbon can eventually support glucose synthesis, but fumarate itself is directly recognised as a TCA cycle intermediate.

bio-073.why: Arginase hydrolyses arginine to urea and ornithine. Ornithine then re-enters mitochondria to take part in another turn of the urea cycle.

notes.A: Citrulline is an earlier intermediate that combines with aspartate to make argininosuccinate.
notes.B: Argininosuccinate is split into arginine and fumarate. The arginine produced is the immediate substrate for urea release.
notes.D: Ornithine is the other product of the arginase reaction and is recycled, rather than being hydrolysed to release urea.

bio-074.why: Methionine is an essential amino acid because humans cannot synthesise enough to meet normal requirements. It must be obtained from the diet and can supply methyl groups through S-adenosylmethionine.

notes.A: Aspartate can be produced by transamination of oxaloacetate and therefore is not an essential dietary amino acid in ordinary conditions.
notes.B: Tyrosine can be made from the essential amino acid phenylalanine when phenylalanine hydroxylase functions normally.
notes.D: Serine can be synthesised from a glycolytic intermediate through a pathway beginning with 3-phosphoglycerate.

bio-075.why: Arginine is conditionally essential. Endogenous synthesis can meet the needs of many healthy adults, but dietary supply can become important in growth or other circumstances when requirements exceed production.

notes.A: Valine is a branched-chain essential amino acid that normally has to be supplied in the diet.
notes.C: Lysine is an essential amino acid rather than one ordinarily synthesised in sufficient amounts by humans.
notes.D: Threonine is an essential amino acid and is normally obtained from dietary protein.

bio-077.why: Valine has a branched hydrocarbon side chain, so it is hydrophobic and nonpolar. The other listed side chains contain hydroxyl or amide groups that can interact with water.

notes.A: Serine has a hydroxyl group in its side chain, making it polar and able to form hydrogen bonds.
notes.C: Asparagine has an uncharged amide side chain that can hydrogen-bond with water or neighbouring groups.
notes.D: Threonine contains a hydroxyl group. Despite its methyl group, it is usually classified as polar uncharged.

bio-078.why: Isoleucine is both ketogenic and glucogenic. Its breakdown yields acetyl-CoA, which can contribute to ketone formation, and propionyl-CoA, which can contribute to glucose production through succinyl-CoA.

notes.A: Valine is glucogenic because its carbon is channelled toward succinyl-CoA, rather than yielding a ketogenic product.
notes.B: Cysteine can be degraded to pyruvate, so it is classified as glucogenic in the standard nutritional scheme.
notes.D: Glycine can contribute to gluconeogenesis, for example after conversion to serine. It is not the ketogenic amino acid in this list.

bio-079.why: Threonine has an oxygen-containing hydroxyl group and no sulphur in its side chain. Cysteine and methionine contain sulphur. Cystine is an oxidised pair of cysteine residues joined by a disulphide bond.

notes.A: Cysteine contains a thiol group, which can form disulphide bonds with another cysteine residue.
notes.B: Cystine contains two sulphur atoms in its disulphide linkage and can occur within folded proteins.
notes.C: Methionine has a sulphur atom in its thioether side chain.

bio-080.why: Tyrosine contains a phenolic aromatic ring. This places it with aromatic amino acids, while the hydroxyl group also confers polarity and can participate in hydrogen bonding.

notes.A: Lysine has an aliphatic chain ending in a basic amino group. It does not contain an aromatic ring.
notes.C: Taurine is an amino sulfonic acid without an aromatic ring and is not a standard residue in proteins.
notes.D: Arginine has a basic guanidinium side chain rather than an aromatic ring.

bio-081.why: Most nitrogen released from amino acid breakdown is converted by the liver into urea. Urea is water soluble and is excreted by the kidneys, making it the main nitrogenous product of protein metabolism in urine.

notes.B: Glutamine transports nitrogen safely between tissues and can support renal ammonium production. It is not the major form excreted.
notes.C: Ammonium excretion is important in acid–base regulation. Urea normally accounts for a larger share of urinary nitrogen.
notes.D: Uric acid mainly comes from purine breakdown rather than being the major product of amino acid nitrogen disposal.

bio-082.why: Glutamate decarboxylase removes carbon dioxide from glutamate to form gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. The enzyme uses pyridoxal phosphate, and GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.

notes.B: Glutathione is a tripeptide formed by joining glutamate, cysteine and glycine. It is not the decarboxylation product of glutamate.
notes.C: Histamine is made by decarboxylation of histidine rather than glutamate.
notes.D: Serotonin is synthesised from tryptophan through hydroxylation followed by decarboxylation.

bio-083.why: Transdeamination couples transamination to oxidative deamination. Amino groups are first transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate, and glutamate dehydrogenase can then release the nitrogen as ammonia.

notes.A: The assertion is correct, but the reason names decarboxylation instead of the initial transamination step.
notes.B: The first step is amino-group transfer, not loss of carbon dioxide. The reason is therefore not a true description of the sequence.
notes.D: Transdeamination does generate ammonia, so the assertion is true even though the reason states the wrong first step.
notes.E: The reason is inaccurate, but the assertion correctly identifies a route for generating ammonia through more than one reaction.

bio-085.why: The urea cycle consumes three ATP molecules per urea, equivalent to four high-energy phosphate bonds. Two ATP are used to make carbamoyl phosphate and another is converted to AMP during argininosuccinate synthesis.

notes.A: Ureogenesis is energy demanding, but the reason omits the ATP used during argininosuccinate synthesis.
notes.B: Both statements cannot be accepted because the whole cycle consumes more than the two ATP used at its entry step.
notes.D: The assertion is true. The stated cost is incomplete because a further ATP is cleaved to AMP.
notes.E: Three ATP molecules are consumed overall, so the reason is inaccurate but the assertion about energy cost is correct.

bio-086.why: The urea cycle spans two compartments. Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and formation of citrulline occur in mitochondria. The later three reactions that convert citrulline to urea and regenerate ornithine occur in the cytosol.

notes.A: Only two of the usual five reactions occur in mitochondria. They do not make up the majority of the steps.
notes.B: The mitochondrial count is two, not four, and the later reactions occur in the cytosol.
notes.C: The assertion about predominant mitochondrial location is incorrect because most of the standard reactions are cytosolic.
notes.D: The proposed count is incorrect. Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and citrulline formation are the two mitochondrial reactions.

bio-087.why: Oxaloacetate can condense with acetyl-CoA to form citrate, provide gluconeogenic carbon after conversion to phosphoenolpyruvate, or accept an amino group to form aspartate. Its fate depends on tissue and metabolic state.

notes.A: Citrate formation is one fate, but oxaloacetate can also support glucose synthesis or be transaminated to aspartate.
notes.B: Condensation and gluconeogenesis are valid. Aspartate aminotransferase also converts oxaloacetate to aspartate.
notes.C: Glucose synthesis and aspartate formation are possible, and citrate synthase also uses oxaloacetate as a substrate.
notes.D: Citrate and aspartate are valid products. Oxaloacetate can also supply carbon for gluconeogenesis.

bio-088.why: Glutamate dehydrogenase can use NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ in oxidative deamination, releasing ammonia and forming alpha-ketoglutarate. The reaction is reversible. High energy signals such as GTP generally inhibit oxidative deamination, while ADP can activate the enzyme.

notes.A: A pyridine nucleotide is used for oxidation, and the enzyme can also catalyse the reverse reaction under suitable conditions.
notes.C: The reaction is reversible, but a high-energy state does not generally stimulate oxidative deamination. The nucleotide acceptor is also required.
notes.D: NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ can support oxidative deamination. High GTP inhibits the enzyme rather than providing the proposed stimulation.
notes.E: The first two statements describe cofactor use and reversibility. The claim about stimulation by a high ATP or GTP state is the error.

bio-089.why: Excess ammonia can disrupt mitochondrial energy production and neurotransmission. In settings such as cirrhosis, hyperammonaemia can also impair skeletal muscle protein synthesis. The effects depend on the affected tissue and severity.

notes.A: Protein synthesis can be impaired, but energy metabolism and nervous system function can also be affected.
notes.B: Ammonia can alter protein synthesis and ATP metabolism, and disturbed neurotransmission is also an important feature of toxicity.
notes.C: Impaired energy production and neural signalling are recognised effects. Hyperammonaemia can also interfere with muscle protein synthesis.
notes.D: Ammonia can impair protein synthesis and neural function. It can additionally disrupt pathways that support ATP production.

bio-090.why: Cysteine catabolism can yield pyruvate, and oxidative pathways through cysteinesulfinate can yield taurine. Glutathione also contains cysteine, but synthesis incorporates the intact amino acid rather than degrading its carbon skeleton.

notes.A: Pyruvate is one product of cysteine degradation. Cysteine can also provide the carbon backbone for taurine.
notes.C: Taurine can be made from cysteine. Glutathione synthesis uses intact cysteine, rather than catabolising the skeleton to glutathione.
notes.D: Pyruvate can result from cysteine catabolism, whereas glutathione is assembled from intact amino acid residues. Taurine is also a valid fate.
notes.E: This group mixes products of cysteine catabolism with a peptide formed by incorporation of intact cysteine.

bio-091.why: Folic acid contains a substituted pteridine ring joined to para-aminobenzoic acid and a glutamate residue. The amino acid component is glutamic acid rather than glutamine.

notes.A: Para-aminobenzoic acid is a component, but folic acid also contains a substituted pteridine ring.
notes.C: The pteridine component is present. The attached amino acid is glutamate, not its amide glutamine.
notes.D: Para-aminobenzoic acid is present, but glutamine is not the amino acid component. This combination also omits the pteridine ring.
notes.E: The ring and para-aminobenzoic acid are correct components. Adding glutamine makes the combination inaccurate.

bio-093.why: Isoleucine yields acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA, while tyrosine yields acetoacetate and fumarate. Each supplies both ketogenic and glucogenic products. Serine is glucogenic through its conversion to pyruvate.

notes.A: Isoleucine is mixed, but tyrosine also supplies both a ketogenic product and a glucogenic product.
notes.C: Tyrosine is mixed, whereas serine yields pyruvate as a glucogenic product. This grouping also leaves out isoleucine.
notes.D: Serine is not conventionally ketogenic. Tyrosine is a mixed amino acid and is missing from this grouping.
notes.E: Isoleucine and tyrosine belong in the mixed group. Serine is classified as glucogenic.

bio-094.why: Isoleucine breakdown yields acetyl-CoA directly. Tryptophan can yield acetoacetyl-CoA and tyrosine yields acetoacetate. Their ketogenic products can give rise to acetyl-CoA during further metabolism, although the immediate breakdown products differ.

notes.A: Tyrosine provides an indirect route through acetoacetate, but isoleucine and tryptophan also provide ketogenic carbon.
notes.B: Isoleucine yields acetyl-CoA and tryptophan yields a ketogenic product. Tyrosine also supplies ketogenic carbon through acetoacetate.
notes.C: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply ketogenic products. Isoleucine provides acetyl-CoA directly as well.
notes.D: This pair gives two examples, but tryptophan also provides ketogenic carbon through acetoacetyl-CoA.

bio-095.why: Serine and cysteine have uncharged polar side chains under usual physiological conditions. Serine has a hydroxyl group and cysteine a thiol group. Methionine has a thioether and is conventionally grouped with nonpolar amino acids.

notes.A: Serine is polar and uncharged, but cysteine also belongs in this category.
notes.C: Cysteine belongs in the polar uncharged group. Methionine's thioether side chain is usually classified as nonpolar.
notes.D: Serine is polar and uncharged, whereas methionine is grouped with nonpolar residues. Cysteine is missing.
notes.E: Cysteine and serine have polar functional groups. Methionine is excluded because its side chain is conventionally nonpolar.

bio-096.why: Arginine has a guanidinium side chain that remains positively charged at physiological pH. Glutamine has an uncharged amide side chain, while glutamate carries a negative side-chain charge.

notes.B: Arginine is positive, but glutamine's side-chain amide has no net charge at physiological pH.
notes.C: Glutamine is uncharged and glutamate is negatively charged. Neither belongs to the basic, positively charged group.
notes.D: Glutamate has a carboxylate side chain and is negatively charged, unlike the guanidinium group of arginine.
notes.E: All three side chains are polar, but only arginine is positively charged under ordinary physiological conditions.

bio-306.why: Many unusual residues in proteins come from modification of a standard amino acid after translation. For example, prolyl hydroxylase acts on proline residues in collagen. The enzymes responsible for such modifications are themselves encoded by genes.

notes.A: The assertion applies to many modified residues, but their modifying enzymes do have genetic coding.
notes.B: Hydroxylation of proline illustrates the assertion. The reason is false because the modifying enzyme is encoded by DNA.
notes.D: The premise about modification is valid for residues such as hydroxyproline. The claim about absent coding for the enzymes is false.
notes.E: The reason is false, but post-translational modification of common amino acids is a recognised source of unusual residues.

bio-397.why: Mammalian glutamate dehydrogenase is regulated allosterically. ADP can activate it, while GTP generally inhibits it. The reason incorrectly assigns the same effect to both nucleotides.

notes.A: Both nucleotides affect the enzyme, but GTP is an inhibitory signal rather than an activator.
notes.B: The reason is inaccurate because the directions of GTP and ADP regulation differ.
notes.D: The enzyme is demonstrably allosteric, and the proposed activation by high GTP is incorrect.
notes.E: The assertion is supported by nucleotide regulation. The error is the stated effect of GTP.

bio-398.why: Aminotransferases use tightly bound pyridoxal phosphate as a prosthetic group. It temporarily accepts an amino group to form pyridoxamine phosphate, then transfers the group to an alpha-keto acid and regenerates pyridoxal phosphate.

notes.B: Tight association with the aminotransferase is consistent with its role as the enzyme's prosthetic group during amino transfer.
notes.C: Pyridoxal phosphate is indeed a tightly associated coenzyme of these transaminases, making the reason true.
notes.D: The assertion is true because pyridoxal phosphate participates directly in the two-stage transfer of the amino group.
notes.E: Both statements describe a recognised feature of pyridoxal phosphate-dependent aminotransferases.

bio-403.why: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a glycolytic metabolite. Aldolase cleaves its carbon–carbon bond to form glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The enzyme fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase performs a separate hydrolysis during gluconeogenesis.

notes.A: The metabolite is not an enzyme and therefore does not belong to the hydrolase class. It is a substrate for aldolase.
notes.B: The reason is correct, but the assertion confuses the metabolite with the enzyme that hydrolyses it.
notes.C: The assertion is false because fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a substrate. Aldol cleavage of it does occur in glycolysis.
notes.E: The assertion is incorrect, but aldolase does cleave fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two triose phosphates.

bio-441.why: Lysine is nutritionally essential in humans because there is no pathway that can synthesise enough lysine for normal needs. Dietary protein therefore supplies the lysine required for protein synthesis and other metabolic functions.

notes.B: Dependence on dietary supply is the basis for classifying lysine as an essential amino acid.
notes.C: Humans cannot make sufficient lysine endogenously, so the reason correctly explains its essential status.
notes.D: Lysine is an essential amino acid, making the assertion as well as the reason true.
notes.E: Both statements are supported by human nutritional requirements for lysine.

bio-442.why: Dietary fructose is already a monosaccharide and does not require digestion into smaller sugars. It enters intestinal epithelial cells chiefly through GLUT5 and exits toward portal blood chiefly through GLUT2.

notes.B: Being a monosaccharide explains why fructose can be absorbed without prior hydrolysis, though transport across enterocytes is still required.
notes.C: Fructose is a dietary monosaccharide. It is distinct from disaccharides such as sucrose that require hydrolysis.
notes.D: Fructose can reach portal blood after transport across intestinal cells, so the assertion is valid in the usual nutritional sense.
notes.E: The two statements describe a monosaccharide that can be absorbed without enzymatic digestion, using specific transporters.

bio-901.why: A larger amino acid load increases the need to dispose of nitrogen through carbamoyl phosphate and urea. Ornithine transcarbamylase is mitochondrial in humans. Each urea requires three ATP molecules, equivalent to four high-energy phosphate bonds.

notes.A: The amino acid load can increase ureagenesis. The energy cost of four high-energy phosphate bonds is also correct.
notes.B: Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis responds to amino acid nitrogen load, but ornithine transcarbamylase is not a human cytosolic urea-cycle enzyme.
notes.C: The energy cost is correct. The location of ornithine transcarbamylase is mitochondrial, and amino acid intake can increase pathway flux.
notes.E: The cytosolic-location statement is false. Increased nitrogen disposal and the four-bond energy cost both apply.

bio-097.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency can cause phenylalanine accumulation, urinary phenylketones and reduced pigmentation from altered tyrosine and melanin metabolism. Tetrahydrobiopterin disorders can also produce hyperphenylalaninaemia by limiting a cofactor required by the hydroxylase.

notes.A: Impaired phenylalanine hydroxylation can affect pigmentation, but phenylpyruvate excretion and cofactor-related disorders are also pertinent.
notes.B: Hypopigmentation and phenylketonuria fit classic hydroxylase deficiency. A shortage of tetrahydrobiopterin can also limit hydroxylation.
notes.C: Both phenylketones and cofactor defects are relevant, and pigmentation can be lighter in untreated classic disease.
notes.D: Pigmentation and tetrahydrobiopterin are relevant. The abnormal phenylalanine pool can also generate urinary phenylpyruvate.

bio-098.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Deficiency leads to excess phenylalanine, some of which is metabolised to phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate.

notes.A: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinaemia type I and accumulation of metabolites such as succinylacetone.
notes.B: Tyrosine 3-monooxygenase makes L-DOPA in catecholamine synthesis. Its deficiency does not explain accumulation of phenylketones.
notes.D: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency disrupts homocysteine metabolism. It is unrelated to the phenylalanine hydroxylation step.

bio-099.why: Leucine, valine and isoleucine are first converted to their corresponding branched-chain alpha-keto acids. Maple syrup urine disease impairs the shared dehydrogenase complex that normally processes all three.

notes.A: Leucine is affected, but the same dehydrogenase complex processes the products of valine and isoleucine catabolism.
notes.B: Leucine and valine belong to the affected group. Isoleucine also requires the shared enzyme complex.
notes.C: Valine and isoleucine are relevant, but leucine metabolism is also disrupted and is especially important in the disease.
notes.D: Leucine and isoleucine are affected. Valine generates a third branched-chain keto acid processed by the same complex.

bio-101.why: Type III tyrosinaemia results from 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase deficiency. Type I causes hepatorenal disease and increases liver cancer risk because fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase is deficient. Type II instead results from tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency.

notes.A: The enzyme defect in type III is correctly described. Type I also carries the stated hepatic and renal risks.
notes.C: The type I complications are correct. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency belongs to type I, rather than type II.
notes.D: Type III involves the dioxygenase. Type II involves tyrosine aminotransferase, and this grouping leaves out the characteristic type I complications.
notes.E: The descriptions of types I and III are correct, but the enzyme assigned to type II actually belongs to type I.

bio-102.why: Tyrosinaemia type II results from tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency. Characteristic findings include painful eye lesions and thickened skin on the palms or soles. Some affected people also have intellectual disability. Seizures are more characteristic of type III.

notes.A: Intellectual disability can occur, but the eye and skin findings are particularly characteristic of type II.
notes.C: Eye and skin lesions fit type II. Seizures are more characteristic of type III, and intellectual disability is also possible in type II.
notes.D: Intellectual disability can be associated with type II. The characteristic combination also includes corneal and skin lesions, not seizures.
notes.E: The first two features fit the typical type II description. Seizures do not belong to its defining clinical pattern.

bio-103.why: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinic aciduria, and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency causes hyperammonaemia. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency impairs citrulline formation and is associated with low or inappropriately normal citrulline, rather than citrullinaemia.

notes.A: The early ornithine transcarbamylase block reduces citrulline formation. Citrullinaemia is typically associated with argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency.
notes.B: Argininosuccinic aciduria does result from the lyase defect, but ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency does not typically raise citrulline.
notes.D: Hyperammonaemia occurs with the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I defect. The ornithine transcarbamylase pairing remains incorrect.
notes.E: The final two pairings are valid. The first pairing incorrectly associates ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency with citrulline accumulation.

bio-107.why: Inborn errors of metabolism are genetic, but their age of presentation varies with residual function and physiological demands. Some present in the newborn period, while others emerge later or become apparent during illness, fasting or a particular dietary exposure.

notes.A: Some disorders present early, but residual enzyme activity can delay the first symptoms until childhood or adulthood.
